title: Beyond the Rasgulla War: How Sun-Dried Mango Powers Odisha's Overlooked Cuisine
excerpt: Ambula — salted, sun-dried mango — quietly anchors Odia cooking, lending a sour depth to curries, chutneys, and rice dishes that most Indian food lovers have never encountered.
body:
• Ambula, salted green mango dried in sunlight for several days, is the cornerstone souring agent in Odia cuisine, used in curries, chutneys, dals, and as a side dish with Pakhala Bhata — fermented rice — during Odisha's summers.
  • While the Rasgulla GI tag battle between Odisha and West Bengal drew national attention, Odisha's broader culinary tradition remains underexplored, built on mustard paste, the five-spice blend Panch Phutana, and the Satvik philosophy of the Jagannath Temple.
  • Food writers and chefs are calling for greater recognition of Odia cuisine, which emphasizes minimal oil, natural flavors, and seasonal preservation techniques honed over centuries.

The Rasgulla war between Odisha and West Bengal made national headlines. Bengal received a Geographical Indication tag for "Banglar Rasogolla" in 2017; Odisha secured its own GI tag for "Odisha Rasagola" in 2019. But the dispute over a single dessert obscured something more interesting — an entire culinary tradition that most of India, let alone the diaspora, has barely explored. At the center of that tradition sits an ingredient so modest it barely registers as one: ambula, sun-dried mango.

What Ambula Is and Why It Matters

Ambula is made from sour green mangoes. The skin is removed, the flesh is mixed with salt, and the pieces are dried in sunlight for several days before being stored in earthen pots called atika. The result is a concentrated souring agent — sweet, tangy, and deeply savory — that functions as a building block across Odia cooking the way tamarind does in South Indian kitchens or dried lime does in Persian cuisine.

Its uses are remarkably versatile. Ambula Rai, perhaps the most celebrated preparation, cooks the dried mango in mustard paste with green chilies, jaggery, and beaten curd, tempered with Panch Phutana — the five-spice blend of cumin, mustard, fenugreek, aniseed, and kalonji that is the signature aromatic base of Odia cuisine. The dish is sweet, sour, and sharp in a single spoonful. Ambula also appears in fish curries, okra stir-fries, and the tangy broth called charu that accompanies rice meals across the state.

A Cuisine Built on Subtlety

Odia cooking operates on a different frequency than the butter-heavy gravies of the north or the coconut-rich curries of the south. It uses minimal oil. It favors mustard paste over cream. Many traditional dishes, inspired by the Mahaprasad offerings at the Jagannath Temple in Puri, are prepared entirely without onion or garlic — a Satvik philosophy that prioritizes the pure flavor of each ingredient.

Dalma, the lentil stew cooked with seasonal vegetables like pumpkin, raw banana, and ridge gourd, tempered with Panch Phutana and finished with grated coconut, is the cuisine's most accessible gateway dish. Pakhala Bhata — rice fermented overnight in water with a hint of curd — is the state's probiotic answer to scorching summers, served with badi chura, crushed sun-dried lentil dumplings mixed with onion, garlic, and green chilies. Chhena Poda, a caramelized cheesecake of fresh cottage cheese, semolina, and cardamom baked in an earthen oven, predates Western cheesecakes by centuries.

"Pakhala is not just food. It cools your body, cleans your soul. Without Pakhala, Odisha summer is impossible."

— Street vendor in Odisha

Preservation as Tradition

Sun-drying is not a single technique in Odisha but an entire philosophy of eating. Beyond ambula, communities across the state dry mushrooms, bamboo shoots, fish, and shrimp to extend their shelf life through lean seasons. The Chuktia Bhunjia community in western Odisha uses a slow smoke-drying method, arranging mushrooms and fish on bamboo racks over a low fire covered with cloth, producing preserved ingredients that last for months. Hendua, dried bamboo shoots, can keep for two to three years when properly stored, and is turned into chutneys with tomatoes and green chilies during winter.

What's Next

For the Indian diaspora, Odia cuisine represents an undiscovered corner of the food they thought they knew. Ambula is rarely found in Indian grocery stores abroad, but the mango-drying technique is simple enough to replicate at home during summer, and several Odia food creators are building online followings with recipes that translate traditional village cooking for modern kitchens. The Rasgulla war got the clicks. The rest of Odisha's table is still waiting for its turn.
